claims.text: The entropy of ideal configurational mixing is maximized when all alloy components have equal atomic fractions.
Increasing configurational entropy contributes to stabilization of a random solid-solution phase and reduces the tendency to form multiphase or ordered structures.
Equimolar high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles retain a single-phase solid solution at high temperatures because of their maximized configurational entropy.
Maximized configurational entropy suppresses the thermodynamic driving force for atomic diffusion.
A deviation from equimolar composition decreases configurational mixing entropy.
A 5–10% deviation in the atomic ratio of one component lowers configurational entropy enough to promote phase separation.
Decreased mixing entropy increases the thermodynamic drive for atomic diffusion and elemental segregation at elevated temperature.
The equimolar nanoparticles will remain homogeneous and single-phase throughout 473–1923 K.
Non-equimolar nanoparticles will exhibit phase separation at a lower temperature than otherwise comparable equimolar nanoparticles.
Non-equimolar nanoparticles will form secondary phases earlier during heating than equimolar nanoparticles.
Both the equimolar and slightly non-equimolar Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Cu nanoparticle batches can initially be prepared as homogeneous single-phase solid solutions.
The predicted stability difference applies in both inert and reactive catalytic or thermoelectric environments.
Matching particle-size distributions and excluding strong metal-support interactions or surface coatings are sufficient to isolate configurational entropy as the cause of any stability difference.
Local ordering may affect segregation behavior independently of the proposed configurational-entropy effect.
